newsitem.title: JAPAN: DLR SLIPS VS YEN ON MARK CROSS SALES AT TOKYO NOON.
newsitem.headline: DLR SLIPS VS YEN ON MARK CROSS SALES AT TOKYO NOON.

text.p: 0300 GMT TRADED HIGH/LOW AS OF 0300 GMT
The dollar slipped against the yen by midday in Tokyo on Friday, pressured by persistent mark selling against the yen in cross trade, dealers said.

The mark fell against the yen as a Japanese life insurer sold a sizeable amount of the German currency, leaving banks that received the orders with mark long positions and forcing them to sell dollars for yen to hedge, said a bank dealer.
The mark was quoted around 63.22/25 yen at 0319 GMT, down from an earlier high around 63.49 yen.
The German currency recovered overseas partly on mark buying against sterling after it set a fresh two-year low of 62.73 yen in Tokyo on Thursday.

"The mark is still vulnerble to declines and there are many willing to sell into rebounds here," said a dealer at a European bank. Uncertanity over the single European currency and a weak German economy have also clouded the prospects for the mark. The mark selling in cross trade helped push the dollar up against the mark by midday Tokyo trade, dealers said.
Another European bank dealer said there were solid bids below 1.8650 marks after overnight declines.
Trading was mostly centred on mark-related transactions during the morning.
Some traders noted that activity was thinning out ahead of the Japanese Obon period next week when many Japanese companies will be closed for a summer holiday.

Japan's June current account surplus data released early in the day also failed to set a clear direction for dollar/yen trade, even though it came out at the top end of market expectations, dealers said.

The Finance Ministry said on Friday Japan's current account surplus, the broadest measure of trade in goods and services, jumped 55.8 percent from a year earlier to 1.02 trillion yen in June, rising for the third consecutive month.
Economists' forecasts for the data had ranged from 840 billion yen to 1.1 trillion yen.

"It was at the top of the range, but not surprising," said a bank dealer. "Concerns about trade friction with the U.S. have persisted, but people are now paying attention to fundamental factors such as declines in stock prices and yen bond yields," he added.
A Japanese bank dealer said Japanese investors are interested in buying dollars on dips.
"I think that a climb in the dollar to 120 yen is still possible next week and the only concern is how monetary authorities will view such a rise," he added.
The dollar closed at 118.38/48 yen and 1.8685/95 marks in New York on Thursday.
